newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's biggest corporate scandal comes to trial.
newsitem.headline: Germany's biggest corporate scandal comes to trial.

text.p: Disgraced tycoon Juergen Schneider goes on trial in Frankfurt on Monday, accused of fraud that led to the collapse of his property empire in one of Germany's biggest corporate scandals.

Schneider, held in a Frankfurt jail since he was extradited from the U.S. last year, insists creditor banks were to blame for the bankruptcy of his group under more than five billion marks ($3 billion) of debt.

It is unclear whether officials of major banks, embarrassed by the apparent ease with which they doled out their billions, will be called to the witness stand. Prosecutors have said they found no evidence of wrongdoing by his banks.
"No witnesses have been summoned, we will first listen to Mr Schneider's testimony," said Job Tilmann, spokesman for the Frankfurt prosecutor's office.

Prosecutors allege Schneider, whose group invested in some of Germany's most prestigious real estate, fooled banks into extending credit by overstating rent income from his properties and by forging bills.
He has been charged with credit fraud, serious fraud and a bankruptcy offence but will not initially be tried for the latter offence, prosecutors said.
If found guilty he faces a maximum sentence of 15 years but any sentence is expected to be far shorter.
The tycoon, a bricklayer who became one of Germany's most celebrated entrepreneurs, gained fame by refurbishing historic hotels and stylish shopping malls in the post-unification property boom.
But his rental income was too low to repay his debts.
The collapse in 1994 sparked fears of a German real estate slump, left hundreds of small craftsmen fighting for their livelihoods and exposed his banks to public outrage.
Deutsche Bank AG, which bore the brunt of criticism for loose lending and lax supervision, accepted the resignations of four executives as a result of the debacle.
But it maintained they had not behaved dishonourably.

Deutsche, Schneider's largest creditor with an exposure of about 1.2 billion marks, made matters worse for itself when its chief executive Hilmar Kopper dismissed as "peanuts" millions of marks Schneider owed to small tradesmen and builders.
Schneider and his wife Claudia disappeared in April 1994, sparking an international manhunt. They were arrested in Miami, Florida, a year later.
Claudia Schneider is accused of abetment to a bankruptcy offence and will stand trial at later. She has been released from prison.
